STEP 1 - Scene: A single whole apple resting on a white square plate, photographed from directly above (top-down view) on a metal-framed stand. This is not a full meal; it is one piece of fruit.

STEP 2 - Ruler: The white plate is a square dinner-style plate, roughly 26 cm across its width. Using a dinner plate of about 26 cm diameter, vessel area is about 3.14 x (13)^2 ≈ 530 cm^2. The apple's width is about one-fifth to one-quarter of the plate width, so roughly 5.5-6.5 cm in diameter, consistent with a medium apple.

STEP 3 - Items: One whole red-and-yellow apple (fresh, raw). No oil, dressing, or sauce is visible.

STEP 4 - Area: The apple's top-down footprint is about 30 cm^2, roughly 6% of the plate area. The food covers only about 6% of the vessel.

STEP 5 - Volume: A whole apple is a roughly spherical solid, not a flat pile. Its outer envelope is about 6 cm in diameter, so volume ≈ (4/3) x 3.14 x 3^3 ≈ 113 ml. Apples are dense, so the bulk density reduction is applied in the next step.

STEP 6 - Grams: Whole fruit is nearly solid, so its effective density is close to 1 g/ml. Using the fruit-piece range for a whole fruit with some internal air, I take about 0.85 g/ml: 113 ml x 0.85 ≈ 96 g. A medium apple typically weighs about 150-180 g, so the visual estimate is lower; I keep the measured-volume estimate of about 100 g, since the apple looks slightly smaller than a standard medium one against the plate.

STEP 7 - Energy: Raw apple is about 52 kcal per 100 g. 100 g x 52 kcal/100 g ≈ 52 kcal.

STEP 8 - Sanity check: A single apple of about 100 g and roughly 50 kcal is plausible. It is a small amount, consistent with one visible apple on a large plate.
